title: Should YOU Write a Book About Teaching?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart takes up a question he says he's asked often: whether a teacher with a persistent urge to write a book about their craft should actually do it. His answer is a qualified yes — if the compulsion has recurred more than ten times, it's worth taking seriously as a calling rather than dismissing as a whim. He illustrates the payoff with three examples: Jim Burke, whose decades of writing and teaching reinforce each other; a pseudonymous teacher ("Edward") who turned burnout into a book of poems and rediscovered purpose in the process; and Sheri Steelman, who capstoned her career with a book on teaching Shakespeare. He's equally candid about the cost, naming several specific difficulties: writing exposes your own lack of clarity, invites imposter syndrome, doesn't make you superior to non-writing colleagues, and can feel futile against the scale of the internet. He closes with an Orwell quotation on the misery of book-writing, agreeing with it while insisting the "grueling" work still helps the person doing it.
points: Offers a specific threshold for taking a book-writing urge seriously: if it's recurred more than ten times, treat it as a real calling, not a whim.
Uses three contrasting case studies (Jim Burke, "Edward," Sheri Steelman) to show book-writing paying off at different career stages and for different reasons.
Names concrete costs of writing about teaching — confronting your own unclarity, imposter syndrome, false superiority — rather than romanticizing the process.
Closes on the idea that book-writing "does something inside" the writer regardless of the book's reception, reframing the labor as self-directed rather than audience-directed.
quotes: If writing a book about teaching is something you've thought about more than ten times, then let's start with: Yes — I think you should take the compulsion seriously.
But the thing to take away is that writing about teaching did something inside of them that not writing about teaching could not.

Writing confronts you with your lack of clarity. It's one thing to have amazing conversations about pedagogy with your hallway colleagues or folks at a conference. Conversations like these are critical to creating great books, but they aren't enough to produce good work.

Writing about teaching will make you feel like an imposter. When you're in the book-writing process, your heart becomes especially sensitive to the ways in which your teaching practice is lacking, especially in comparison to others.
Just because I'm an oddball who sometimes finds himself compelled to write books doesn't mean I'm of any greater value than the fearfully and wonderfully wrought colleague down the hall.

Writing a book is a horrible, exhausting struggle, like a long bout of some painful illness. One would never undertake such a thing if one were not driven on by some demon whom one can neither resist nor understand.
